title: Container Security
summary: Container security covers the full lifecycle of an image and the container it becomes: base image provenance, dependency and malware scanning, build hardening, registry access control, admission policy at deploy time, runtime isolation and monitoring, plus the security of the orchestrator that schedules everything. A container is not a security boundary by default, because containers share the host kernel and rely on namespaces, control groups and system call filtering for isolation. A kernel flaw, or an over-privileged container such as one with the runtime socket mounted, can therefore reach the host. That is why the orchestrator control plane, not the container, is normally the highest-value target: whoever controls the scheduler can run code everywhere. Container security appears in supply chain discussions, in platform engineering work, and in incident response after a cryptomining workload suddenly appears in a cluster. The mistake is equating it with image scanning alone, then running images as root, with mutable tags and no admission controls.

beginner.definition: A container is a light package that holds a program and everything it needs to run. Container security means keeping that package safe from the moment it is built until it stops running. You check the parts inside it, the settings it runs with, and the place it runs. A container is not a strong wall by itself, so it needs careful rules.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many containers share one operating system kernel, so a weakness in one can affect the others. A single bad library inside an image can appear in hundreds of copies across your company. Containers are also easy to start quickly, which means a wrong setting can spread faster than any review. Attackers target the management system that controls containers, because it can reach everything. Good container security limits how far one broken container can go.
howItWorks: Start with a small, trusted base image and record which version you used, instead of pulling the newest tag.
Scan the image for known weak libraries during the build, and stop the build when the risk is too high.
Run the process as a normal user rather than as the system administrator, and remove tools it does not need.
Limit the container at run time with read only file systems and simple permission rules.
Let only approved images run, using a policy that checks where the image came from and how it was signed.
Watch the running containers and the management system for strange processes, new admin roles and unexpected connections.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat where each person has their own room. The rooms are separate, but everyone uses the same front door, the same water pipes and the same electricity. If one person leaves a tap running, everyone suffers. Container security is the flat rules. You check what each person brings in, you lock the front door properly, and you watch the shared spaces. The room walls are thin, so you do not rely on them alone.
takeaways: A container shares the host system, so treat it as a packaging tool and not as a wall.
Control what goes into the image and what that image may do while it runs.
Protect the management system, because whoever controls it controls every container.

objectives: Explain what a container is and where security controls apply across its lifecycle.
Describe why containers provide weaker isolation than separate machines.
Identify risks in images, in runtime settings and in the orchestrator control plane.
Outline controls such as trusted base images, scanning, admission policy and least privilege.
Describe how container activity is monitored and investigated after an incident.
